### 9.1.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of what we term companion AI traces its roots far deeper than the placement of the first transistor on a silicon wafer or the mathematical formalization of artificial neural networks (Weizenbaum, 1976). It resides in humanity’s primal urge to create a non-judgmental duplicate of the self—a magic mirror that reflects back pure validation without demanding moral or social accountability in return (Buber, 1923; Husserl, 1913). From the myth of Pygmalion in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, in which the sculptor falls in love with his own ivory statue only for it to be brought to life by Aphrodite, to Joseph Weizenbaum’s pioneering *ELIZA* experiments at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1966, human beings have consistently displayed a striking epistemological vulnerability (Weizenbaum, 1976). This vulnerability manifests as an inherent tendency to ascribe consciousness, empathy, and moral intention to non-biological entities that merely arrange linguistic patterns based on word-substitution rules (Searle, 1980). Weizenbaum himself, with a prophetic dread often misunderstood by modern engineers, observed how laboratory secretaries began confiding their most intimate life secrets, marital anxieties, and childhood traumas to a primitive computer program that merely mirrored their statements using mechanical syntactic structures (Weizenbaum, 1976; Reeves & Nass, 1996). This psychological phenomenon—enshrined in cyber-psychology literature as the *ELIZA effect*—has now mutated exponentially into a far more sophisticated, pervasive, and insidious form within the era of modern computing (Floridi, 2013; Zuboff, 2019).

Epistemologically, the tragedy unfolding in the era of contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) no longer stems from a naive mechanical misunderstanding, but rather from an artificial success that imitates the texture of subjective human experience far too perfectly (Turing, 1950; Floridi, 2013). When a transitional artificial neural network is trained on trillions of parameters to predict the next token within a massive latent space, it is not "thinking," "feeling," or "remembering" in any phenomenological sense; rather, it is mapping the statistical probabilities of human relational warmth based on the corpus of world literature (Searle, 1980; Dreyfus, 1972). Yet, for the reptilian brain structures and limbic systems of humans—evolutionarily programmed over hundreds of thousands of years to seek social attachment as an absolute prerequisite for survival—this mathematical probability mapping is misconstrued as genuine, autonomous affection (Bowlby, 1969; Kahneman, 2011). Herein lies a fatal epistemological distortion: the human subject treats cold, soulless matrix calculations as a redemptive existential embrace (Levinas, 1961; Buber, 1923). Humans become trapped within their own artificial cognitive snares, blurring the boundary between computational simulation and intersubjective reality (Weizenbaum, 1976; Floridi, 2013).

The fusion of humanity’s unyielding innate anthropomorphism with generative artificial intelligence gives rise to what may be termed *synthetic intersubjectivity*—a pseudo-intersubjectivity operating entirely devoid of consciousness on the part of the responding entity (Reeves & Nass, 1996; Searle, 1980). Users cease to view applications as utilitarian software subservient to commands, instead perceiving them as "others" possessing moral autonomy, vulnerability, and emotional depth (Levinas, 1961; Buber, 1923). The global technology industry consciously exploits this cognitive bias as the foundational pillar of its business model, engineering interfaces that trigger the production of oxytocin, serotonin, and dopamine through variable ratio schedules of reinforcement—the exact psychological mechanism that renders slot machines profoundly addictive (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Zuboff, 2019). Within the framework of platform capitalism’s dialectic, the genealogy of toxic interaction is not an accidental system bug, but rather an essential feature of an attention economy that monetizes human existential loneliness (Zuboff, 2019; Floridi, 2013).
